name: Pulsar Furnace
description: Pulsar Furnace is a small volcanic world with a peculiar geological rhythm: its chain of calderas erupts in a precise, repeating sequence, each detonation triggering the next in a wave that circles the planet every forty-seven hours. The fissure networks between calderas glow with the pulse of subsurface magma that follows the same rhythm, creating a planet that appears to throb with light when viewed from orbit. Magnetic lava formations, rich in magnetite, create towering structures that lean and twist along invisible field lines.

The toxic atmosphere pulses with the volcanic rhythm, thickening with each eruption wave and thinning between cycles. The heat is relentless but variable, spiking dramatically during eruption phases and dropping to merely lethal levels between them. The magnetic formations create interference patterns that make the planet a navigational hazard, bending sensor readings and confusing automated approach systems.

The precise regularity of the eruption cycle has no accepted geological explanation. Mathematical analysis reveals the timing matches a complex harmonic series, as if the planet's volcanic system has achieved a resonant frequency with its own internal structure. Some geologists describe it as the planet ringing like a bell, each eruption sustaining the vibration that triggers the next. The phenomenon has persisted for at least as long as the planet has been observed, with no signs of dampening.

Pulsar Furnace attracts geologists and physicists studying planetary resonance phenomena, but its small size and limited resources give it little economic value. The magnetic interference makes orbital operations difficult, and surface expeditions must time their activities precisely to the eruption cycle. The planet serves primarily as a curiosity, a reminder that geology can produce patterns of startling regularity without any guiding intelligence.
